name: Pitcairn Islands
summary_text: The Pitcairn Islands stand under the United Kingdom's framework: defence and external affairs are reserved to the United Kingdom, and United Kingdom domestic measures such as the Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not apply here of their own force. Local law governs, and those measures could reach Pitcairn only by Order in Council. Military service is likewise a United Kingdom responsibility rather than a local one.  Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001.  The Pitcairn Constitution Order 2010 prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, and that guarantee has been in force since 2010.  Same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015. The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 defines marriage as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity. The Island Council approved the ordinance unanimously on 1 April 2015; Governor Jonathan Sinclair signed it on 5 May 2015 and it was published on 13 May 2015.  The same ordinance recognises civil partnerships performed outside Pitcairn. Adoption has been legal since 2015 and is open to married, unmarried and single people.  None of the roughly 50 residents is known to be in a same-sex relationship.

sources.title: Laws of Pitcairn 1893 and Laws of 1904 by R. T. Simons
sources.documents: 1893 Laws did not mention homosexuality; 1904 laws made it a crime for unmarried persons of either sex to congregate together causing scandal or endangering morals of younger members
sources.detail: Notes Pitcairn placed under jurisdiction of High Commissioner for Western Pacific in 1898. No URL visible in provided text.

name: Philippines
summary_text: The Philippines does not criminalise same-sex relations or trans identity, and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender. Same-sex relations have never been criminalised. A 2026 travel-risk assessment scores Manila at 69 of 100, 'Generally Safe', for LGBTQ+ travellers overall, but 62 for trans travellers, which falls in the 'Exercise Caution' band; the same assessment scores HIV-positive travellers at 81.  No administrative legal gender recognition process exists. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048, 2001) bars an administrative birth-certificate sex change for trans people, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery. A bill filed by trans Filipinos would permit applicants, including consenting minors, to choose markers other than male or female, such as X or non-binary; it had not been enacted as of the reports, which allies planned to endorse to the 20th Congress on 28 July. The Commission on Human Rights has described that year's killings of trans people as a disturbing pattern of transfemicide.  No national SOGI anti-discrimination statute is in force. The SOGIE Equality Bill has been pending in Congress for roughly 25 years, since 2000, without passage. The protections that do exist form a patchwork: SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances in eight provinces, including Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur and Iloilo, and in 32 cities and municipalities, alongside sectoral statutes. The Magna Carta for Public Social Workers penalises SOGIE harassment with a fine of 20,000 to 40,000 pesos and/or up to one year's imprisonment; the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act punish transphobic, homophobic and misogynistic slurs and ridicule with fines of 1,000 to 10,000 pesos, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar. Republic Act 11166 prohibits discrimination tied to HIV status, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression.  Violence against trans people is documented and recent. In June 2025 two killings occurred within days: 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol was found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June after being reported missing, and a trans woman former journalist and activist was shot by an unidentified gunman inside a clinic in General Santos the same day. In May 2025 a foreign national was arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas. In April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd at a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan; she called the attack traumatic, and the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community. Bahaghari cited the June 2025 cases as an urgent reason to pass the SOGIE Equality Bill.  Detention carries acute risk. Transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories in Philippine jails, including Manila City Jail, where head-shaving on arrival is mandatory for the male dorm and safety depends on inmate hierarchies rather than policy; informal same-sex pairings are used by gangs as a survival and protection strategy against abuse. There is no gender-matched placement. Official practice instead takes the form of administrative segregation: the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology in Davao transfers LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex, alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, to prevent abuse.  Local ordinances restrict presentation in public. Marawi City banned men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings in December 2004, and Kabacan in Cotabato prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments, and cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence. After the 2017 Marawi siege, people perceived as LGBTQ were at times harassed in displacement camps.  Social visibility is high. Long-standing gender-diversity traditions with local names such as bakla and tomboy sit alongside prominent Pride events and nightlife and substantial LGBTQ+ media presence. Openly gay and bisexual people have been permitted in the armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017, with uniform policy following the legal gender recorded on the birth certificate. The lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. Marriage equality does not exist; in June 2023 Quezon City launched the country's first Right to Care Card, letting registered LGBTQ couples make medical and health decisions for each other, initially in government-owned hospitals.

In April 2024 the drag artist Taylor Sheesh was struck on stage by a man from the crowd at a concert in Bayambang, Pangasinan; she called the attack traumatic, and the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community. Bahaghari cited the June 2025 cases as an urgent reason to pass the SOGIE Equality Bill.  Detention carries acute risk. Transgender women and gay men are held in ordinary male dormitories in Philippine jails, including Manila City Jail, where head-shaving on arrival is mandatory for the male dorm and safety depends on inmate hierarchies rather than policy; informal same-sex pairings are used by gangs as a survival and protection strategy against abuse. There is no gender-matched placement. Official practice instead takes the form of administrative segregation: the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology in Davao transfers LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex, alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens, to prevent abuse.  Local ordinances restrict presentation in public. Marawi City banned men from appearing in public in female attire, makeup or earrings in December 2004, and Kabacan in Cotabato prohibited cross-dressing and homosexual relations for Muslims in November 2019 under penalty of imprisonment. Gender-diverse people have been refused entry and service by establishments, and cross-dressers and transgender people may be excluded from private and public spaces with little or no legal consequence. After the 2017 Marawi siege, people perceived as LGBTQ were at times harassed in displacement camps.  Social visibility is high. Long-standing gender-diversity traditions with local names such as bakla and tomboy sit alongside prominent Pride events and nightlife and substantial LGBTQ+ media presence. Openly gay and bisexual people have been permitted in the armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017, with uniform policy following the legal gender recorded on the birth certificate. The lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility was updated in 2023 to bar discrimination against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. Marriage equality does not exist; in June 2023 Quezon City launched the country's first Right to Care Card, letting registered LGBTQ couples make medical and health decisions for each other, initially in government-owned hospitals.
